57	The vibration device 10 may include one or more handles 44, as shown in FIG. 1. The handle 44 is arranged to guide the vibration device 10 over the exposed face 38 while the pressure differential holds the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36. The handle 44 serves primarily to guide the vibration device 10 rather than to press it against the covering element 36, because the contact load is supplied by the pressure differential. The handle 44 is shown schematically in FIG. 1.
58

60	
61	FIG. 5 shows a second embodiment. A flexible pulling element 46 is connected to the vibration device 10. The flexible pulling element 46 is a rope, wire, cable or similar flexible pulling element. The vibration device 10 is translatable over the exposed face 38 by tension applied to the flexible pulling element 46 while the pressure differential is maintained: the operator applies that tension and the vibration device 10 slides on the bearing face 26 in the direction of the applied tension.
62	
63	This embodiment gives decoupled control. The flexible pulling element 46 moves the vibration device 10 across the exposed face 38 when the operator applies tension to it. The force holding the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36 is supplied independently, and continuously, by the pressure differential across the base 12. Position is thus controlled by one agency and contact by another: the operator sets where the vibration device 10 is with a small pulling force, while the quality of the vibration coupling is set by the air-extraction mechanism 20 and is supplied independently of the tension applied to the flexible pulling element 46.
64	
65	Method of use
66	
67	A method of bedding a covering element 36 into bonding material 40 using the vibration device 10 is carried out as follows. The method begins with placing the vibration device 10 on the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36, whereby the bearing face 26 of the perimeter member 24 is brought against the exposed face 38 so that the chamber 22 is bounded by the second side 16, the perimeter member 24 and the exposed face 38, with the clearance 34 remaining, along at least part of the perimeter member 24, between the bearing face 26 and the exposed face 38. It continues with operating the air-extraction mechanism 20 to withdraw air from the chamber 22 at a volumetric extraction rate sufficient to maintain the chamber 22 below atmospheric pressure while ambient air continues to enter the chamber 22 through the clearance 34, the resulting pressure differential holding the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36 without a downward force being required from the operator. It continues with operating the vibration motor 18 and transmitting vibration from the vibration motor 18 to the covering element 36 through the base 12 and the perimeter member 24 to the bearing face 26. It continues with translating the vibration device 10 across the exposed face 38, while the pressure differential is maintained, by sliding the bearing face 26 over the exposed face 38, so that vibration is delivered to successive areas of the covering element 36. The translating may be done by applying tension to the flexible pulling element 46, or by guiding the vibration device 10 with the handle 44.

tool_use_result.originalFile:
A vibration device is disclosed for bedding a covering element into thinset, mortar, adhesive or similar bonding material. The device has a rigid base with a first side and a second side. A vibration motor is coupled to the first side. An air-extraction mechanism is coupled to the first side and is in fluid communication with a chamber on the second side. A perimeter member extends from the second side at a perimeter of that side, runs around the chamber, and terminates in a bearing face that rests on the exposed face of the covering element. The perimeter member is rigid and of a low-friction material such as plastic, metal, polytetrafluoroethylene, or a combination of rigid materials, and the bearing face is the end face of that member.

The perimeter member is not a seal and is not asked to behave like one. When the bearing face rests on the exposed face, a clearance remains along at least part of the perimeter member through which ambient air passes continuously into the chamber. The perimeter member restricts that flow without stopping it. The air-extraction mechanism withdraws air from the chamber at a volumetric extraction rate sufficient to maintain the chamber below atmospheric pressure while ambient air continues to enter through the clearance. The resulting pressure differential acts over the area of the chamber and presses the device against the covering element.

Two consequences follow, and they are the point of the arrangement. First, the force holding the device down is supplied by the pressure differential rather than by the operator, so the operator need not press the device against the covering element, and the loaded, vibrating path from tool to hand is avoided rather than damped. Second, every member in the path from the vibration motor to the covering element, namely the base and the perimeter member terminating in the bearing face, is rigid, with no elastomeric or foam element interposed, so the vibration crosses into the covering element with substantially less damping than through a flexible suction cup. The device is thus coupled to the covering element without an intervening compliant member or air film, while the operator's hands carry less.

Because the member that touches the covering element is a rigid low-friction bearing face rather than a gripping cup, the device can be translated across the exposed face while the pressure differential is being maintained. Holding and sliding are not alternative modes to be switched between: the same continuously running extraction keeps the device down while it is moved, so vibration can be delivered at successive positions over the covering element without the hold ever being released and without the vibration amplitude falling away with distance from a fixed attachment point.

In one embodiment the device carries one or more handles, which serve to guide and steer the device rather than to press it down. In another embodiment a flexible pulling element such as a rope, wire or cable is attached to the device, and the operator moves the device by pulling on that element. This gives decoupled control: the position of the device is set by a small pulling force applied by the operator, while the force holding the device against the covering element, and with it the quality of the vibration coupling, is set independently and constantly by the pressure differential.

A method of bedding a covering element using the device, and a system comprising the device together with the flexible pulling element, are also disclosed.

In the following description, the same reference numeral denotes the same part throughout the drawings. The embodiments described are examples and do not limit the scope of what is claimed.

Overview

FIG. 1 shows a vibration device 10 in use, FIG. 2 shows it in vertical section, and FIG. 4 shows the bedded layers beneath it in enlarged detail. A covering element 36, which may be a tile or other covering material, has been laid onto a bed of bonding material 40 spread over a substrate 42, as seen in FIG. 4. The bonding material 40 may be thinset, mortar, tile adhesive or any similar bonding material. The substrate 42 is the surface being covered. The covering element 36 presents an exposed face 38 facing away from the bonding material 40. The vibration device 10 rests on the exposed face 38 and delivers vibration into the covering element 36, which drives trapped air out of the bonding material 40, distributes the bonding material 40 more evenly beneath the covering element 36, increases the area of contact between the covering element 36 and the bonding material 40, and strengthens the bond between the covering element 36 and the substrate 42.

The vibration device 10 comprises a base 12, a vibration motor 18, an air-extraction mechanism 20 and a perimeter member 24. The base 12 is rigid and has a first side 14 facing away from the covering element 36 and a second side 16 opposite the first side 14 and facing the covering element 36. The vibration motor 18 is coupled to the first side 14. The air-extraction mechanism 20 is also coupled to the first side 14 and is in fluid communication with a chamber 22 located on the second side 16. The perimeter member 24 extends from the second side 16 at a perimeter of the second side 16, runs around the chamber 22, and terminates in a bearing face 26 that contacts the exposed face 38.

The base

The base 12 is rigid: under the alternating force produced by the vibration motor 18 and under the pressure differential described below, the base 12 is not compliant, and it transmits the vibration to the perimeter member 24 with substantially less damping than a flexible suction cup would.

The second side 16 of the base 12 forms the upper boundary of the chamber 22. The chamber 22 is in fluid communication with the air-extraction mechanism 20.

The vibration motor

The vibration motor 18 is coupled to the first side 14 of the base 12, with no elastomeric member, foam member or resilient mount interposed between the vibration motor 18 and the base 12. That direct coupling is intentional. A resilient motor mount would isolate the base 12 from the vibration motor 18, which is the opposite of what is wanted: the entire object of the device is to put vibration into the covering element 36, and any compliant member anywhere between the vibration motor 18 and the exposed face 38 removes energy from that transfer.

The vibration motor 18 produces mechanical vibration in the base 12.

The air-extraction mechanism

The air-extraction mechanism 20 is coupled to the first side 14 of the base 12, as seen in FIG. 2, and withdraws air from the chamber 22. In the embodiment shown, the air-extraction mechanism 20 is a vacuum pump carried on the base 12.

The air-extraction mechanism 20 runs continuously while the vibration device 10 is in use. It is not run to establish a vacuum and then stopped: the chamber 22 is never sealed, so the pressure differential exists only while the air-extraction mechanism 20 withdraws air from the chamber 22.

The perimeter member and the chamber

The perimeter member 24 stands proud of the second side 16 and surrounds the chamber 22: a rigid loop, or skirt, that runs round the second side 16 at its perimeter. As shown in FIG. 3, the perimeter member 24 is a closed loop running around the second side 16 at its perimeter. The perimeter member 24, the second side 16 of the base 12 and, in use, the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36 together bound the chamber 22. The chamber 22 is a single space bounded by one perimeter member 24, as shown in FIG. 2. The perimeter member 24 is rigidly connected to the base 12 at the second side 16, and vibration passes from the base 12 into the perimeter member 24 with substantially less damping than through a flexible suction cup.

The perimeter member 24 terminates, at its end remote from the base 12, in a bearing face 26 that contacts the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36. The perimeter member 24 is made of a low-friction rigid material, and the bearing face 26 is the end face of that member, so that the face bearing on the exposed face 38 is of that low-friction material. Suitable materials are plastic, metal, polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE), and combinations of rigid materials.

The perimeter member 24 is not a seal. It is free of rubber, elastomer and foam. This distinguishes it from a suction cup and from a compliant sealing skirt, and the difference is functional rather than nominal. A suction cup works by conforming to the surface, closing the enclosed space against the atmosphere, and holding the reduced pressure inside; conforming requires compliance, and compliance in the load path damps vibration. The perimeter member 24 is instead hard and dimensionally stable, and it makes rigid contact with the exposed face 38.

Because the perimeter member 24 is not intended to form a complete airtight seal, a clearance 34 remains between the bearing face 26 and the exposed face 38 along at least part of the perimeter member 24, as shown enlarged in FIG. 4. The clearance 34 is shown enlarged for clarity. FIG. 2 is taken through places along the perimeter member 24 at which the perimeter member 24 bears on the covering element 36, and FIG. 4 is taken at a place along the perimeter member 24 at which the clearance 34 is present. The enlarged detail of FIG. 4 also shows the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36, and the covering element 36 bedded in the bonding material 40 that has been spread over the substrate 42. Ambient air passes through the clearance 34 into the chamber 22 continuously while the vibration device 10 is in use. The clearance 34 is not a defect to be eliminated. It is the condition the vibration device 10 is designed to work in: the perimeter member 24 restricts the flow of ambient air into the chamber 22 without closing that path.

The pressure differential that holds the device down

The air-extraction mechanism 20 withdraws air from the chamber 22 at a volumetric extraction rate sufficient to maintain the chamber 22 below atmospheric pressure while ambient air continues to enter through the clearance 34, for as long as the air-extraction mechanism 20 runs.

The difference between atmospheric pressure and the pressure in the chamber 22, acting over the plan area of the chamber 22, produces a holding force that presses the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36. The holding force is sufficient to hold the vibration device 10 against the exposed face 38 without any downward force being applied by an operator. The contact load is therefore supplied by the pressure differential rather than by the operator's hands.

The vibration device 10 can be translated across the exposed face 38 while the pressure differential is being maintained. The pressure differential is maintained continuously throughout the translating, so that the vibration device 10 is held against the covering element 36 and slid over the exposed face 38 at the same time; holding and sliding are simultaneous, not alternatives. The bearing face 26, being of a low-friction material, is slidable over the exposed face 38 while the pressure differential is maintained, and the air-extraction mechanism 20 continues to run and continues to hold the vibration device 10 down throughout the movement. No grip has to be released and re-established. Vibration can therefore be delivered to successive areas of the covering element 36, instead of the vibration intensity falling away with distance from a single fixed attachment point.

The vibration transmission path

The vibration transmission path runs as follows. Vibration produced by the vibration motor 18 passes into the base 12 at the first side 14, along the base 12, into the perimeter member 24 at the second side 16, along the perimeter member 24, and out through the bearing face 26 into the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36. Every member in that path, namely the base 12 and the perimeter member 24 terminating in the bearing face 26, is rigid, and no elastomeric member, foam member or resilient mount is interposed anywhere along it. The vibration therefore reaches the covering element 36 with substantially less damping than it would in an arrangement in which a flexible suction cup, a resilient motor mount or a vibration-damping handle lies in the path.

The holding force from the pressure differential also acts to keep the bearing face 26 in contact with the exposed face 38. Contact is maintained by a force that does not vary with what the operator is doing, which is what makes the transfer consistent across the working area.

The clearance 34 does not separate the bearing face 26 from the covering element 36 over the whole of the loop, in the way that a film of air, where such a film remains, separates a pressed-on sliding base from the covering element beneath it. Where a film of that kind remains beneath a sliding base of that kind, it lies between that sliding base and the covering element beneath it over the whole area of that sliding base, so that what crosses the interface crosses the film, and the film may dampen the vibration crossing it. Here the bearing face 26 is loaded onto the exposed face 38 by the holding force and bears rigidly on it, and the vibration is carried across that rigid contact. The clearance 34, present along at least part of the perimeter member 24, admits ambient air into the chamber 22 without the bearing face 26 being separated from the exposed face 38 by an intervening compliant member. Nothing compressible is interposed in the load path, and the holding force presses the contact together rather than holding the two faces apart.

The force balance on the vibration device 10 in use is as follows. The weight of the vibration device 10 and the holding force act downward on the covering element 36; the reaction of the exposed face 38 acts upward; the frictional resistance of the bearing face 26 acts in the plane of the exposed face 38 and opposes translation; and the force the operator need supply is an in-plane force sufficient to overcome that frictional resistance and to steer. Because no downward force is required from the operator, no loaded path need be maintained from the vibrating device into the operator's hands, wrists, arms and joints. The vibration reaching the operator is reduced not by absorbing it in a damper, which would take the same energy away from the covering element 36, but by removing the operator from the load path altogether. The usual trade-off, in which stronger coupling to the covering element 36 is bought with greater hand pressure and therefore with greater vibration exposure, does not arise here: the coupling is set by the air-extraction mechanism 20 and the operator's grip has nothing to do with it.

Handles

The vibration device 10 may include one or more handles 44, as shown in FIG. 1. The handle 44 is arranged to guide the vibration device 10 over the exposed face 38 while the pressure differential holds the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36. The handle 44 serves primarily to guide the vibration device 10 rather than to press it against the covering element 36, because the contact load is supplied by the pressure differential. The handle 44 is shown schematically in FIG. 1.

Embodiment with a flexible pulling element

FIG. 5 shows a second embodiment. A flexible pulling element 46 is connected to the vibration device 10. The flexible pulling element 46 is a rope, wire, cable or similar flexible pulling element. The vibration device 10 is translatable over the exposed face 38 by tension applied to the flexible pulling element 46 while the pressure differential is maintained: the operator applies that tension and the vibration device 10 slides on the bearing face 26 in the direction of the applied tension.

This embodiment gives decoupled control. The flexible pulling element 46 moves the vibration device 10 across the exposed face 38 when the operator applies tension to it. The force holding the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36 is supplied independently, and continuously, by the pressure differential across the base 12. Position is thus controlled by one agency and contact by another: the operator sets where the vibration device 10 is with a small pulling force, while the quality of the vibration coupling is set by the air-extraction mechanism 20 and is supplied independently of the tension applied to the flexible pulling element 46.

Method of use

A method of bedding a covering element 36 into bonding material 40 using the vibration device 10 is carried out as follows. The method begins with placing the vibration device 10 on the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36, whereby the bearing face 26 of the perimeter member 24 is brought against the exposed face 38 so that the chamber 22 is bounded by the second side 16, the perimeter member 24 and the exposed face 38, with the clearance 34 remaining, along at least part of the perimeter member 24, between the bearing face 26 and the exposed face 38. It continues with operating the air-extraction mechanism 20 to withdraw air from the chamber 22 at a volumetric extraction rate sufficient to maintain the chamber 22 below atmospheric pressure while ambient air continues to enter the chamber 22 through the clearance 34, the resulting pressure differential holding the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36 without a downward force being required from the operator. It continues with operating the vibration motor 18 and transmitting vibration from the vibration motor 18 to the covering element 36 through the base 12 and the perimeter member 24 to the bearing face 26. It continues with translating the vibration device 10 across the exposed face 38, while the pressure differential is maintained, by sliding the bearing face 26 over the exposed face 38, so that vibration is delivered to successive areas of the covering element 36. The translating may be done by applying tension to the flexible pulling element 46, or by guiding the vibration device 10 with the handle 44.

In the following description, the same reference numeral denotes the same part throughout the drawings. The embodiments described are examples and do not limit the scope of what is claimed.

Overview

FIG. 1 shows a vibration device 10 in use, FIG. 2 shows it in vertical section, and FIG. 4 shows the bedded layers beneath it in enlarged detail. A covering element 36, which may be a tile or other covering material, has been laid onto a bed of bonding material 40 spread over a substrate 42, as seen in FIG. 4. The bonding material 40 may be thinset, mortar, tile adhesive or any similar bonding material. The substrate 42 is the surface being covered. The covering element 36 presents an exposed face 38 facing away from the bonding material 40. The vibration device 10 rests on the exposed face 38 and delivers vibration into the covering element 36, which drives trapped air out of the bonding material 40, distributes the bonding material 40 more evenly beneath the covering element 36, increases the area of contact between the covering element 36 and the bonding material 40, and strengthens the bond between the covering element 36 and the substrate 42.

The vibration device 10 comprises a base 12, a vibration motor 18, an air-extraction mechanism 20 and a perimeter member 24. The base 12 is rigid and has a first side 14 facing away from the covering element 36 and a second side 16 opposite the first side 14 and facing the covering element 36. The vibration motor 18 is coupled to the first side 14. The air-extraction mechanism 20 is also coupled to the first side 14 and is in fluid communication with a chamber 22 located on the second side 16. The perimeter member 24 extends from the second side 16 at a perimeter of the second side 16, runs around the chamber 22, and terminates in a bearing face 26 that contacts the exposed face 38.

The base

The base 12 is rigid: under the alternating force produced by the vibration motor 18 and under the pressure differential described below, the base 12 is not compliant, and it transmits the vibration to the perimeter member 24 with substantially less damping than a flexible suction cup would.

The second side 16 of the base 12 forms the upper boundary of the chamber 22. The chamber 22 is in fluid communication with the air-extraction mechanism 20.

The vibration motor

The vibration motor 18 is coupled to the first side 14 of the base 12, with no elastomeric member, foam member or resilient mount interposed between the vibration motor 18 and the base 12. That direct coupling is intentional. A resilient motor mount would isolate the base 12 from the vibration motor 18, which is the opposite of what is wanted: the entire object of the device is to put vibration into the covering element 36, and any compliant member anywhere between the vibration motor 18 and the exposed face 38 removes energy from that transfer.

The vibration motor 18 produces mechanical vibration in the base 12.

The air-extraction mechanism

The air-extraction mechanism 20 is coupled to the first side 14 of the base 12, as seen in FIG. 2, and withdraws air from the chamber 22. In the embodiment shown, the air-extraction mechanism 20 is a vacuum pump carried on the base 12.

The air-extraction mechanism 20 runs continuously while the vibration device 10 is in use. It is not run to establish a vacuum and then stopped: the chamber 22 is never sealed, so the pressure differential exists only while the air-extraction mechanism 20 withdraws air from the chamber 22.

The perimeter member and the chamber

The perimeter member 24 stands proud of the second side 16 and surrounds the chamber 22: a rigid loop, or skirt, that runs round the second side 16 at its perimeter. As shown in FIG. 3, the perimeter member 24 is a closed loop running around the second side 16 at its perimeter. The perimeter member 24, the second side 16 of the base 12 and, in use, the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36 together bound the chamber 22. The chamber 22 is a single space bounded by one perimeter member 24, as shown in FIG. 2. The perimeter member 24 is rigidly connected to the base 12 at the second side 16, and vibration passes from the base 12 into the perimeter member 24 with substantially less damping than through a flexible suction cup.

The perimeter member 24 terminates, at its end remote from the base 12, in a bearing face 26 that contacts the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36. The perimeter member 24 is made of a low-friction rigid material, and the bearing face 26 is the end face of that member, so that the face bearing on the exposed face 38 is of that low-friction material. Suitable materials are plastic, metal, polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE), and combinations of rigid materials.

The perimeter member 24 is not a seal. It is free of rubber, elastomer and foam. This distinguishes it from a suction cup and from a compliant sealing skirt, and the difference is functional rather than nominal. A suction cup works by conforming to the surface, closing the enclosed space against the atmosphere, and holding the reduced pressure inside; conforming requires compliance, and compliance in the load path damps vibration. The perimeter member 24 is instead hard and dimensionally stable, and it makes rigid contact with the exposed face 38.

Because the perimeter member 24 is not intended to form a complete airtight seal, a clearance 34 remains between the bearing face 26 and the exposed face 38 along at least part of the perimeter member 24, as shown enlarged in FIG. 4. The clearance 34 is shown enlarged for clarity. FIG. 2 is taken through places along the perimeter member 24 at which the perimeter member 24 bears on the covering element 36, and FIG. 4 is taken at a place along the perimeter member 24 at which the clearance 34 is present. The enlarged detail of FIG. 4 also shows the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36, and the covering element 36 bedded in the bonding material 40 that has been spread over the substrate 42. Ambient air passes through the clearance 34 into the chamber 22 continuously while the vibration device 10 is in use. The clearance 34 is not a defect to be eliminated. It is the condition the vibration device 10 is designed to work in: the perimeter member 24 restricts the flow of ambient air into the chamber 22 without closing that path.

The pressure differential that holds the device down

The air-extraction mechanism 20 withdraws air from the chamber 22 at a volumetric extraction rate sufficient to maintain the chamber 22 below atmospheric pressure while ambient air continues to enter through the clearance 34, for as long as the air-extraction mechanism 20 runs.

The difference between atmospheric pressure and the pressure in the chamber 22, acting over the plan area of the chamber 22, produces a holding force that presses the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36. The holding force is sufficient to hold the vibration device 10 against the exposed face 38 without any downward force being applied by an operator. The contact load is therefore supplied by the pressure differential rather than by the operator's hands.

The vibration device 10 can be translated across the exposed face 38 while the pressure differential is being maintained. The pressure differential is maintained continuously throughout the translating, so that the vibration device 10 is held against the covering element 36 and slid over the exposed face 38 at the same time; holding and sliding are simultaneous, not alternatives. The bearing face 26, being of a low-friction material, is slidable over the exposed face 38 while the pressure differential is maintained, and the air-extraction mechanism 20 continues to run and continues to hold the vibration device 10 down throughout the movement. No grip has to be released and re-established. Vibration can therefore be delivered to successive areas of the covering element 36, instead of the vibration intensity falling away with distance from a single fixed attachment point.

The vibration transmission path

The vibration transmission path runs as follows. Vibration produced by the vibration motor 18 passes into the base 12 at the first side 14, along the base 12, into the perimeter member 24 at the second side 16, along the perimeter member 24, and out through the bearing face 26 into the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36. Every member in that path, namely the base 12 and the perimeter member 24 terminating in the bearing face 26, is rigid, and no elastomeric member, foam member or resilient mount is interposed anywhere along it. The vibration therefore reaches the covering element 36 with substantially less damping than it would in an arrangement in which a flexible suction cup, a resilient motor mount or a vibration-damping handle lies in the path.

The holding force from the pressure differential also acts to keep the bearing face 26 in contact with the exposed face 38. Contact is maintained by a force that does not vary with what the operator is doing, which is what makes the transfer consistent across the working area.

The clearance 34 does not separate the bearing face 26 from the covering element 36 over the whole of the loop, in the way that a film of air, where such a film remains, separates a pressed-on sliding base from the covering element beneath it. Where a film of that kind remains beneath a sliding base of that kind, it lies between that sliding base and the covering element beneath it over the whole area of that sliding base, so that what crosses the interface crosses the film, and the film may dampen the vibration crossing it. Here the bearing face 26 is loaded onto the exposed face 38 by the holding force and bears rigidly on it, and the vibration is carried across that rigid contact. The clearance 34, present along at least part of the perimeter member 24, admits ambient air into the chamber 22 without the bearing face 26 being separated from the exposed face 38 by an intervening compliant member. Nothing compressible is interposed in the load path, and the holding force presses the contact together rather than holding the two faces apart.

The force balance on the vibration device 10 in use is as follows. The weight of the vibration device 10 and the holding force act downward on the covering element 36; the reaction of the exposed face 38 acts upward; the frictional resistance of the bearing face 26 acts in the plane of the exposed face 38 and opposes translation; and the force the operator need supply is an in-plane force sufficient to overcome that frictional resistance and to steer. Because no downward force is required from the operator, no loaded path need be maintained from the vibrating device into the operator's hands, wrists, arms and joints. The vibration reaching the operator is reduced not by absorbing it in a damper, which would take the same energy away from the covering element 36, but by removing the operator from the load path altogether. The usual trade-off, in which stronger coupling to the covering element 36 is bought with greater hand pressure and therefore with greater vibration exposure, does not arise here: the coupling is set by the air-extraction mechanism 20 and the operator's grip has nothing to do with it.

Handles

The vibration device 10 may include one or more handles 44, as shown in FIG. 1. The handle 44 is arranged to guide the vibration device 10 over the exposed face 38 while the pressure differential holds the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36. The handle 44 serves primarily to guide the vibration device 10 rather than to press it against the covering element 36, because the contact load is supplied by the pressure differential. The handle 44 is shown schematically in FIG. 1.

Embodiment with a flexible pulling element

FIG. 5 shows a second embodiment. A flexible pulling element 46 is connected to the vibration device 10. The flexible pulling element 46 is a rope, wire, cable or similar flexible pulling element. The vibration device 10 is translatable over the exposed face 38 by tension applied to the flexible pulling element 46 while the pressure differential is maintained: the operator applies that tension and the vibration device 10 slides on the bearing face 26 in the direction of the applied tension.

This embodiment gives decoupled control. The flexible pulling element 46 moves the vibration device 10 across the exposed face 38 when the operator applies tension to it. The force holding the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36 is supplied independently, and continuously, by the pressure differential across the base 12. Position is thus controlled by one agency and contact by another: the operator sets where the vibration device 10 is with a small pulling force, while the quality of the vibration coupling is set by the air-extraction mechanism 20 and is supplied independently of the tension applied to the flexible pulling element 46.

Embodiment with stirring elements

FIG. 6 shows a third embodiment. The vibration device 10 carries one or more stirring elements 48. Because the pressure differential holds the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36 while the bearing face 26 is of a low-friction material, the vibration device 10 is held down and at the same time free to move over the exposed face 38, unlike a device that is gripped at one place. The vibration produced by the vibration motor 18 acts through the stirring elements 48 to produce a constant forward motion of the vibration device 10 over the exposed face 38. The vibration device 10 therefore advances from area to area of the covering element 36 without tension being applied to a flexible pulling element 46 and without being guided by hand, while the pressure differential is maintained throughout. The hold is not loosened to permit that motion: the air-extraction mechanism 20 continues to run and the pressure differential continues to press the bearing face 26 onto the exposed face 38 while the vibration device 10 advances, so the vibration coupling into the covering element 36 is not interrupted by the movement. The stirring elements 48 are shown schematically in FIG. 6.

In this embodiment the operator supplies neither the force that holds the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36 nor the force that moves it across the exposed face 38. The first is supplied by the pressure differential and the second by the vibration of the vibration device 10 acting through the stirring elements 48, so the vibration that is being delivered into the covering element 36 also carries the vibration device 10 over it.

Method of use

A method of bedding a covering element 36 into bonding material 40 using the vibration device 10 is carried out as follows. The method begins with placing the vibration device 10 on the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36, whereby the bearing face 26 of the perimeter member 24 is brought against the exposed face 38 so that the chamber 22 is bounded by the second side 16, the perimeter member 24 and the exposed face 38, with the clearance 34 remaining, along at least part of the perimeter member 24, between the bearing face 26 and the exposed face 38. It continues with operating the air-extraction mechanism 20 to withdraw air from the chamber 22 at a volumetric extraction rate sufficient to maintain the chamber 22 below atmospheric pressure while ambient air continues to enter the chamber 22 through the clearance 34, the resulting pressure differential holding the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36 without a downward force being required from the operator. It continues with operating the vibration motor 18 and transmitting vibration from the vibration motor 18 to the covering element 36 through the base 12 and the perimeter member 24 to the bearing face 26. It continues with translating the vibration device 10 across the exposed face 38, while the pressure differential is maintained, by sliding the bearing face 26 over the exposed face 38, so that vibration is delivered to successive areas of the covering element 36. The translating may be done by applying tension to the flexible pulling element 46, by guiding the vibration device 10 with the handle 44, or by the vibration acting through the stirring elements 48 to advance the vibration device 10 over the exposed face 38.

tool_use_result.originalFile:
When a tile or similar covering element is laid onto a bed of thinset, mortar or adhesive, air is trapped between the covering element and the bonding material and the bonding material is unevenly distributed beneath the covering element. Mechanical vibration applied to the exposed face of the covering element after it is laid drives the trapped air out, spreads the bonding material into a more uniform layer, increases the area over which the bonding material actually touches the covering element, and thereby improves the strength of the completed bond. Hand-guided vibration devices are used for this purpose.

Such devices generally comprise a vibration motor carried on a handle together with one of two arrangements for putting the vibration into the covering element: a smooth sliding base that the operator presses down onto the exposed face, or a flexible suction cup that grips the exposed face at one place. In one known hand-held device for lifting and laying tiles, a handle carries two shafts, an electric motor vibrates the shafts, and a head shell at the free end of each shaft carries a suction cup on its underside, the suction cups being evacuated by an electrically operated pump and each being formed by a rubber-elastic apron [REF:DE-202021002652-U1].

The first of two problems with existing tile vibration devices is that both arrangements couple the vibration into the covering element poorly. A smooth sliding base has to be pressed hard against the covering element by the operator, and even under that pressure a thin film of air can remain between the base and the covering element and damp the vibration crossing the interface. A flexible suction cup makes a firmer connection, but the rubber or foam wall that forms the cup is compliant, and a compliant member placed in the path between the motor and the covering element absorbs and dissipates part of the vibration instead of delivering it. A device gripped by such a cup is also anchored at one place on the covering element: it cannot be slid to another area without first releasing the grip, and the vibration amplitude reaching areas remote from the point of attachment falls off with distance from that point.

Vacuum coupling arrangements used away from tile setting approach the holding of a body against a surface in other ways, each on the terms of its own document. In one adhesion device that holds itself to a wall surface, the peripheral wall of the decompressed space between the base and the wall surface is formed by elastic partitions, of which the partition nearer the wall surface has an end that contacts the wall surface, and a frame member of higher rigidity is added on the partition to restrict the partition from being deformed into that space as it is drawn down [REF:US-11408462-B2]. In a base assembly for coupling an end effector to a structure, a cavity on the second side of the assembly is held to the structure by vacuum drawn by a pneumatic generator operating in a suction mode, and the assembly is moved across the structure substantially frictionlessly on an air cushion produced by the same generator operating in a blower mode, a control being provided that selectively switches the generator between the suction mode and the blower mode [REF:US-10001245-B2]. In a device that suction-adheres to a wall surface and moves along it, a seal member mounted in the main body defines a pressure reduction space in cooperation with the wall surface, vacuum creating means discharges fluid from that space so that the main body adheres by the difference in fluid pressure inside and outside the space, and vibration generating means mounted on the main body imparts a lifting force in a direction away from the wall surface that reduces the suction-adhering force, together with a force along the wall surface that moves the main body [REF:US-4934475-A]. The vibration there is used to loosen the suction-adhering hold and to drive the main body along the wall surface. Vacuum is used differently again in handling equipment, where the object is to pick a workpiece up rather than to hold a tool down on it: in one vacuum plate lifting system for lifting sheet material articles, a substantially horizontal suction plate has a perforated suction lifting surface directed downward for contact with the upper surface of the article, an airflow suction system conveys vacuum air pressure to that surface, a lifter actuation system such as a robotic arm lifts and moves the plate, and an elongate bar movably mounted along an edge of the plate carries nozzles that are lowered to sweep a suction airflow across the surface beneath to remove dust or debris [REF:US-11247858-B2]. That system carries the article away from the work surface and cleans the work surface by suction; it does not deliver vibration into a covering element already laid on a bed of bonding material, and it accordingly says nothing about how a vibrating tool might be kept in contact with such a covering element while it is moved over it.

The second problem with existing tile vibration devices concerns the operator rather than the tile. Because contact has to be maintained by hand, the operator applies substantial and continuous downward force through the handle, and vibration travels back up that loaded path into the hands, wrists, arms and joints, producing discomfort, fatigue and a risk of injury. Shock absorbers and vibration-damping handles reduce some of the vibration reaching the operator, but they do so by absorbing mechanical energy that would otherwise have gone into the covering element, so the tool is made kinder to the operator by being made worse at its job. The two problems are coupled: firmer coupling to the covering element is obtained by pressing harder, and pressing harder is exactly what increases the vibration dose to the operator.

What is needed is a way to hold a vibration device against a covering element with a force that does not come from the operator's arms, to conduct the vibration into the covering element without passing it through any compliant member, and to allow the device to be moved from area to area over the covering element without ever giving up that hold.

The Field again covers devices advanced across the work by their own vibration; the Summary carries the further embodiment; the detailed description has the section "Embodiment with stirring elements", including that the hold is not loosened to permit the motion, and lists the option in the method of use; numeral 48 is back in the table; FIG. 6 is restored with numerals 10, 24, 36 and 48 and its Brief Description entry; claim 10 is the device dependent and claim 20 the method dependent, with the system and method claims renumbered to 11 to 14 and 15 to 19 and every dependency updated, giving 20 claims and 3 independents. A search showed the rollback went further than that one sheet: no stirring elements anywhere, no numeral 48, no FIG. 6 file, and claims back to 18. The inventor's passage adding the autonomous mode is still in input/conversation.md, so the rolled-back candidate no longer matched its own sources.

The request asks to preserve disclosure support and re-review every section and claim. A rebuild that silently dropped an embodiment the inventor asked for would fail that on its face, so restoring it was the substance of this turn rather than an addition of my own.

I restored exactly what the sources support and nothing more: one or more stirring elements carried by the device, vibration acting through them to produce a constant forward motion, and the device advancing without being pulled or guided. No form, count, size, material or mounting location is stated in the application text, and the figure brief again declares the two drawn blocks and their place a per-sheet depiction convention with no mounting face asserted.

The stirring-element claims went back as dependents of claim 1 and claim 15 rather than as new independents, since the autonomous mode works only because of what claim 1 already recites, and both keep the recital that the differential is maintained while the device advances. I inserted the device claim in class order and renumbered the system and method groups so each dependent still follows its parent; the set is 20 claims and 3 independents, inside the fee-free limit.

The claims recite the stirring elements, so they must be shown. FIG. 6 is rebuilt on the FIG. 5 pattern for the same machine, carrying 10, 24, 36 and 48, and the Brief Description gains the matching entry, so the sheet count is six.

Two earlier corrections had been undone by the rollback and I reapplied both: the force-balance sentence again says the operator supplies the in-plane force only where the operator moves the device, which is what keeps it consistent with the autonomous embodiment and claims 10 and 20, and the Background again writes the prior-art tool as that sliding base so the bare noun base stays reserved for the claimed base 12. I verified that the hedged film wording, the antecedent fix in claim 2 and the qualified prior-art wording in the detailed description had survived, and left them alone.

I did not reintroduce section-line designations. The reverted FIG. 3 brief draws no cutting line and states that no lettering is drawn, and both sectional views identify their planes in prose, FIG. 2 through the base, chamber and perimeter member and FIG. 4 at a place where the clearance is present, so the drawing set is internally consistent as it now stands.

The review reports no findings, and its description of sixteen numerals, eighteen claims and five sheets is a record of the older candidate rather than a defect in this one, so nothing in the draft was changed on its account.

Claim 2 keeps the non-sealing, flow-restricting closed loop, which is the sharpest separation from the rubber-elastic apron of DE-202021002652-U1 and the elastic partitions of US-11408462-B2. # FIG. 1 - Perspective view of the vibration device in use

**View:** Perspective view from above and to the front left. Outline line work only, with no lettering drawn.

**Geometry to be drawn**

The covering element 36 is one large plain tile in perspective filling the lower drawing area, the machine standing on its left-hand part with open tile to the right.

The machine is one plain rectangular slab, the base 12, standing on a band that runs round its underside. Three closed blocks stand side by side on the top face of the slab: the left-hand block is the vibration motor 18, the middle block is the handle 44, and the right-hand block is the air-extraction mechanism 20. Slab, band, blocks and tile are shown schematically, and the order and spacing of the three blocks is a placement convention for this sheet only, no particular handle form, size or mounting arrangement being asserted.

The slab is drawn thick, its front face turned toward the viewer as a large plain surface; its proportions are schematic. The view being taken from the front left, the left-hand end of the slab is also presented to the viewer, its outline standing upright from the band below to the top face above.

Each block is drawn broad and tall, its front face turned toward the viewer.

The band meets the underside of the slab and follows the same rectangular run, its front surface facing the viewer as one unbroken strip across the whole width, drawn deep enough for a point to stand well inside it; its depth is schematic. It stands on the tile, its lower edge meeting it.

The whole of the drawing stands well inside the drawing area, the machine drawn large within it.

- The vibration device 10 is the whole machine, slab, blocks and band together. Identified on the upright outline at the left-hand end of the slab, anywhere along it between the band below and the top face above, clear of the front face of the slab.

input.summary: All three failing sheets are repaired in their briefs. FIG. 1: numeral 10 no longer targets an outline where two edges converge; the left-hand end of the slab is now specified as a plain four-sided end face drawn broad enough to hold a point, and numeral 10 targets well inside that face, clear of its edges and of the front face. FIG. 2: the hatching is respecified stroke by stroke rather than by angle alone, each stroke of the slab starting low on the left and ending high on the right like a forward slash, each stroke of both legs starting high on the left and ending low on the right like a backslash so a leg's strokes cross the slab's where they meet, and each stroke of the band steep and close to upright, much nearer to vertical than the legs' strokes. FIG. 6: the band's front strip must now be deep enough at every point across its width to hold a point clear of both edges, and numeral 24 targets well inside the right-hand part of that strip. To hold FIG. 2 within the length limit I compressed eight phrases that repeated wording already in the brief; it is at 2793 characters and every brief is at or below the limit. No claim, numeral definition, drawing description or disclosed embodiment changed.
reasoning: FIG. 1's endpoint failed because the target was a line rather than an area: on a perspective slab the left-hand upright outline meets the top face edge at a corner, so a dot placed along it can land on the vertex. The cure is to give numeral 10 an interior region, and the sheet already presents the slab's left-hand end to the viewer, so naming that end as a four-sided face and drawing it broad enough to hold a point makes the target unambiguous without adding structure. Numeral 12 still takes the front face, so the two remain distinct.

FIG. 2 has now failed on hatch direction through several formulations that specified degrees. Degrees are evidently not what the renderer follows, so I described the strokes themselves: where each stroke begins and ends, with the familiar forward slash and backslash shapes, and the band as steep and close to upright. I also stated the consequence a reviewer looks for, that a leg's strokes cross the slab's where the two meet, which is a positive geometric relationship rather than a rendering prohibition.

Hatch direction is a sectioning convention and carries no technical content, so nothing about the invention moved: the four bodies, the flush legs at the perimeter of the underside, the legs standing on the band, and the broken indicating line that stops at the base faces without asserting a passage are all unchanged.

FIG. 6's numeral 24 sat in a rejected coordinate cluster, which usually means the target region is too shallow to hold a dot reliably. I fixed the cause rather than the coordinate: the front strip of the band must now be deep enough at every point across its width for a point to stand well inside it clear of both edges, and the numeral targets the right-hand part of that strip, away from the blocks the sheet also carries. Right-hand is a stable direction, not an ordinal that could be read either way.
I kept every target broad and removed the old FIG. 6 wording that located the dot by reference to two bounding lines, which is the kind of narrow instruction that produces borderline placements.

The rewritten FIG. 2 brief ran long, so I compressed phrases that repeat what other sentences already carry. Nothing load-bearing was dropped: all four bodies, the hatching assignment, the contacts, the fluid-communication line and all six numeral entries with their tolerance wording remain.
No text file was touched. The failures are all drawing-side, and the application text, claims, numeral table and drawing descriptions already match the six-figure plan restored in the previous turn.

input.prior_art_strategy: Unchanged. Claim 1 rests on the rigid low-friction perimeter member at the perimeter of the second side, ending in a bearing face that leaves a clearance admitting ambient air continuously; an air-extraction mechanism whose volumetric rate holds the chamber below atmospheric against that ingress; an all-rigid transmission path with no elastomeric member, foam member or resilient mount interposed; and a bearing face slidable while the differential is maintained. The FIG. 2 repair matters to that position: hatching that distinguishes the base from the perimeter member and the perimeter member from the covering element keeps the section reading as two rigid parts rigidly connected and bearing on the tile, which is what separates the invention from the rubber-elastic apron of DE-202021002652-U1 and the elastic partitions of US-11408462-B2. Claims 10 and 20 remain dependent and keep the recital that the device advances while the differential is maintained, distinguishing US-4934475-A, whose vibration reduces the suction-adhering hold to permit travel, and US-10001245-B2, which floats on a blower-fed air cushion to move. US-11247858-B2 remains lifting and cleaning equipment that delivers no vibration into a laid covering element.

1. A vibration device for bedding a covering element into a bonding material, the vibration device comprising:

a base that is rigid and has a first side and a second side opposite the first side;

a vibration motor coupled to the first side;

a perimeter member extending from the second side at a perimeter thereof and surrounding a chamber located on the second side, the perimeter member being rigid and of a low-friction material and terminating, remote from the base, in a bearing face that is an end face of the perimeter member, the chamber being bounded by the second side, the perimeter member and, when the bearing face is placed against an exposed face of the covering element, by the exposed face, and a clearance remaining, along at least part of the perimeter member, between the bearing face and the exposed face, through which clearance ambient air enters the chamber; and

an air-extraction mechanism coupled to the first side and in fluid communication with the chamber, the air-extraction mechanism being operable to withdraw air from the chamber at a volumetric extraction rate sufficient to maintain the chamber below atmospheric pressure while the ambient air continues to enter the chamber through the clearance, a resulting pressure differential holding the vibration device against the covering element;

wherein a vibration transmission path from the vibration motor to the bearing face passes through the base and the perimeter member, each member of the vibration transmission path is rigid, and no elastomeric member, foam member or resilient mount is interposed in the vibration transmission path; and

wherein the bearing face is slidable over the exposed face while the pressure differential is maintained.

2. The vibration device of claim 1, wherein the perimeter member is a closed loop that runs around the chamber, the closed loop restricting a flow of the ambient air into the chamber through the clearance without closing the clearance and without forming a complete airtight seal.

3. The vibration device of claim 1, wherein the low-friction material of the perimeter member is plastic, metal, polytetrafluoroethylene, or a combination of rigid materials.

4. The vibration device of claim 1, wherein the perimeter member is free of rubber, elastomer and foam, and makes rigid contact with the exposed face.

5. The vibration device of claim 1, wherein the pressure differential produces a holding force sufficient to hold the vibration device against the exposed face without a downward force being applied by an operator.

6. The vibration device of claim 1, wherein the air-extraction mechanism is operable to withdraw air from the chamber continuously while the vibration device is in use.

7. The vibration device of claim 1, wherein the air-extraction mechanism is a vacuum pump.

8. The vibration device of claim 1, further comprising a handle arranged to guide the vibration device over the exposed face while the pressure differential holds the vibration device against the covering element.

9. The vibration device of claim 1, further comprising a flexible pulling element connected to the vibration device, the vibration device being translatable over the exposed face by tension applied to the flexible pulling element while the pressure differential is maintained.

10. The vibration device of claim 1, further comprising one or more stirring elements carried by the vibration device, wherein vibration from the vibration motor acts through the one or more stirring elements to produce a forward motion of the vibration device over the exposed face while the pressure differential is maintained.

11. A system for bedding a covering element into a bonding material, the system comprising:

a vibration device comprising a base that is rigid and has a first side and a second side opposite the first side, a vibration motor coupled to the first side, a perimeter member extending from the second side at a perimeter thereof and surrounding a chamber located on the second side, and an air-extraction mechanism coupled to the first side and in fluid communication with the chamber,

the perimeter member being rigid and of a low-friction material and terminating, remote from the base, in a bearing face that is an end face of the perimeter member, the chamber being bounded by the second side, the perimeter member and, when the bearing face is placed against an exposed face of the covering element, by the exposed face, and a clearance remaining, along at least part of the perimeter member, between the bearing face and the exposed face, through which clearance ambient air enters the chamber,

the air-extraction mechanism being operable to withdraw air from the chamber at a volumetric extraction rate sufficient to maintain the chamber below atmospheric pressure while the ambient air continues to enter the chamber through the clearance, a resulting pressure differential holding the vibration device against the covering element,

a flexible pulling element connected to the vibration device, the flexible pulling element being arranged to move the vibration device across the exposed face when tension is applied to it,

In the following description, the same reference numeral denotes the same part throughout the drawings. The embodiments described are examples and do not limit the scope of what is claimed.

Overview

FIG. 1 shows a vibration device 10 in use, FIG. 2 shows it in vertical section, and FIG. 4 shows the bedded layers beneath it in enlarged detail. A covering element 36, which may be a tile or other covering material, has been laid onto a bed of bonding material 40 spread over a substrate 42, as seen in FIG. 4. The bonding material 40 may be thinset, mortar, tile adhesive or any similar bonding material. The substrate 42 is the surface being covered. The covering element 36 presents an exposed face 38 facing away from the bonding material 40. The vibration device 10 rests on the exposed face 38 and delivers vibration into the covering element 36, which drives trapped air out of the bonding material 40, distributes the bonding material 40 more evenly beneath the covering element 36, increases the area of contact between the covering element 36 and the bonding material 40, and strengthens the bond between the covering element 36 and the substrate 42.

The vibration device 10 comprises a base 12, a vibration motor 18, an air-extraction mechanism 20 and a perimeter member 24. The base 12 is rigid and has a first side 14 facing away from the covering element 36 and a second side 16 opposite the first side 14 and facing the covering element 36. The vibration motor 18 is coupled to the first side 14. The air-extraction mechanism 20 is also coupled to the first side 14 and is in fluid communication with a chamber 22 located on the second side 16. The perimeter member 24 extends from the second side 16 at a perimeter of the second side 16, runs around the chamber 22, and terminates in a bearing face 26 that contacts the exposed face 38.

The base

The base 12 is rigid: under the alternating force produced by the vibration motor 18 and under the pressure differential described below, the base 12 is not compliant, and it transmits the vibration to the perimeter member 24 with substantially less damping than a flexible suction cup would.

The second side 16 of the base 12 forms the upper boundary of the chamber 22. The chamber 22 is in fluid communication with the air-extraction mechanism 20.

The vibration motor

The vibration motor 18 is coupled to the first side 14 of the base 12, with no elastomeric member, foam member or resilient mount interposed between the vibration motor 18 and the base 12. That direct coupling is intentional. A resilient motor mount would isolate the base 12 from the vibration motor 18, which is the opposite of what is wanted: the entire object of the device is to put vibration into the covering element 36, and any compliant member anywhere between the vibration motor 18 and the exposed face 38 removes energy from that transfer.

The vibration motor 18 produces mechanical vibration in the base 12.

The air-extraction mechanism

The air-extraction mechanism 20 is coupled to the first side 14 of the base 12, as seen in FIG. 2, and withdraws air from the chamber 22. In the embodiment shown, the air-extraction mechanism 20 is a vacuum pump carried on the base 12.

The air-extraction mechanism 20 runs continuously while the vibration device 10 is in use. It is not run to establish a vacuum and then stopped: the chamber 22 is never sealed, so the pressure differential exists only while the air-extraction mechanism 20 withdraws air from the chamber 22.

The perimeter member and the chamber

The perimeter member 24 stands proud of the second side 16 and surrounds the chamber 22: a rigid loop, or skirt, that runs round the second side 16 at its perimeter. As shown in FIG. 3, the perimeter member 24 is a closed loop running around the second side 16 at its perimeter. The perimeter member 24, the second side 16 of the base 12 and, in use, the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36 together bound the chamber 22. The chamber 22 is a single space bounded by one perimeter member 24, as shown in FIG. 2. The perimeter member 24 is rigidly connected to the base 12 at the second side 16, and vibration passes from the base 12 into the perimeter member 24 with substantially less damping than through a flexible suction cup.

The perimeter member 24 terminates, at its end remote from the base 12, in a bearing face 26 that contacts the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36. The perimeter member 24 is made of a low-friction rigid material, and the bearing face 26 is the end face of that member, so that the face bearing on the exposed face 38 is of that low-friction material. Suitable materials are plastic, metal, polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE), and combinations of rigid materials.

The perimeter member 24 is not a seal. It is free of rubber, elastomer and foam. This distinguishes it from a suction cup and from a compliant sealing skirt, and the difference is functional rather than nominal. A suction cup works by conforming to the surface, closing the enclosed space against the atmosphere, and holding the reduced pressure inside; conforming requires compliance, and compliance in the load path damps vibration. The perimeter member 24 is instead hard and dimensionally stable, and it makes rigid contact with the exposed face 38.

Because the perimeter member 24 is not intended to form a complete airtight seal, a clearance 34 remains between the bearing face 26 and the exposed face 38 along at least part of the perimeter member 24, as shown enlarged in FIG. 4. The clearance 34 is shown enlarged for clarity. FIG. 2 is taken through places along the perimeter member 24 at which the perimeter member 24 bears on the covering element 36, and FIG. 4 is taken at a place along the perimeter member 24 at which the clearance 34 is present. The enlarged detail of FIG. 4 also shows the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36, and the covering element 36 bedded in the bonding material 40 that has been spread over the substrate 42. Ambient air passes through the clearance 34 into the chamber 22 continuously while the vibration device 10 is in use. The clearance 34 is not a defect to be eliminated. It is the condition the vibration device 10 is designed to work in: the perimeter member 24 restricts the flow of ambient air into the chamber 22 without closing that path.

The pressure differential that holds the device down

The air-extraction mechanism 20 withdraws air from the chamber 22 at a volumetric extraction rate sufficient to maintain the chamber 22 below atmospheric pressure while ambient air continues to enter through the clearance 34, for as long as the air-extraction mechanism 20 runs.

The difference between atmospheric pressure and the pressure in the chamber 22, acting over the plan area of the chamber 22, produces a holding force that presses the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36. The holding force is sufficient to hold the vibration device 10 against the exposed face 38 without any downward force being applied by an operator. The contact load is therefore supplied by the pressure differential rather than by the operator's hands.

The vibration device 10 can be translated across the exposed face 38 while the pressure differential is being maintained. The pressure differential is maintained continuously throughout the translating, so that the vibration device 10 is held against the covering element 36 and slid over the exposed face 38 at the same time; holding and sliding are simultaneous, not alternatives. The bearing face 26, being of a low-friction material, is slidable over the exposed face 38 while the pressure differential is maintained, and the air-extraction mechanism 20 continues to run and continues to hold the vibration device 10 down throughout the movement. No grip has to be released and re-established. Vibration can therefore be delivered to successive areas of the covering element 36, instead of the vibration intensity falling away with distance from a single fixed attachment point.

The vibration transmission path

The vibration transmission path runs as follows. Vibration produced by the vibration motor 18 passes into the base 12 at the first side 14, along the base 12, into the perimeter member 24 at the second side 16, along the perimeter member 24, and out through the bearing face 26 into the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36. Every member in that path, namely the base 12 and the perimeter member 24 terminating in the bearing face 26, is rigid, and no elastomeric member, foam member or resilient mount is interposed anywhere along it. The vibration therefore reaches the covering element 36 with substantially less damping than it would in an arrangement in which a flexible suction cup, a resilient motor mount or a vibration-damping handle lies in the path.

The holding force from the pressure differential also acts to keep the bearing face 26 in contact with the exposed face 38. Contact is maintained by a force that does not vary with what the operator is doing, which is what makes the transfer consistent across the working area.

The clearance 34 does not separate the bearing face 26 from the covering element 36 over the whole of the loop, in the way that a film of air, where such a film remains, separates a pressed-on sliding base from the covering element beneath it. Where a film of that kind remains beneath a sliding base of that kind, it lies between that sliding base and the covering element beneath it over the whole area of that sliding base, so that what crosses the interface crosses the film, and the film may dampen the vibration crossing it. Here the bearing face 26 is loaded onto the exposed face 38 by the holding force and bears rigidly on it, and the vibration is carried across that rigid contact. The clearance 34, present along at least part of the perimeter member 24, admits ambient air into the chamber 22 without the bearing face 26 being separated from the exposed face 38 by an intervening compliant member. Nothing compressible is interposed in the load path, and the holding force presses the contact together rather than holding the two faces apart.

The force balance on the vibration device 10 in use is as follows. The weight of the vibration device 10 and the holding force act downward on the covering element 36; the reaction of the exposed face 38 acts upward; the frictional resistance of the bearing face 26 acts in the plane of the exposed face 38 and opposes translation; and, where the vibration device 10 is moved by the operator, the force the operator need supply is an in-plane force sufficient to overcome that frictional resistance and to steer. Because no downward force is required from the operator, no loaded path need be maintained from the vibrating device into the operator's hands, wrists, arms and joints. The vibration reaching the operator is reduced not by absorbing it in a damper, which would take the same energy away from the covering element 36, but by removing the operator from the load path altogether. The usual trade-off, in which stronger coupling to the covering element 36 is bought with greater hand pressure and therefore with greater vibration exposure, does not arise here: the coupling is set by the air-extraction mechanism 20 and the operator's grip has nothing to do with it.

Handles

The vibration device 10 may include one or more handles 44, as shown in FIG. 1. The handle 44 is arranged to guide the vibration device 10 over the exposed face 38 while the pressure differential holds the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36. The handle 44 serves primarily to guide the vibration device 10 rather than to press it against the covering element 36, because the contact load is supplied by the pressure differential. The handle 44 is shown schematically in FIG. 1.

Embodiment with a flexible pulling element

FIG. 5 shows a second embodiment. A flexible pulling element 46 is connected to the vibration device 10. The flexible pulling element 46 is a rope, wire, cable or similar flexible pulling element. The vibration device 10 is translatable over the exposed face 38 by tension applied to the flexible pulling element 46 while the pressure differential is maintained: the operator applies that tension and the vibration device 10 slides on the bearing face 26 in the direction of the applied tension.

This embodiment gives decoupled control. The flexible pulling element 46 moves the vibration device 10 across the exposed face 38 when the operator applies tension to it. The force holding the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36 is supplied independently, and continuously, by the pressure differential across the base 12. Position is thus controlled by one agency and contact by another: the operator sets where the vibration device 10 is with a small pulling force, while the quality of the vibration coupling is set by the air-extraction mechanism 20 and is supplied independently of the tension applied to the flexible pulling element 46.

Embodiment with stirring elements

FIG. 6 shows a third embodiment. The vibration device 10 carries one or more stirring elements 48. Because the pressure differential holds the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36 while the bearing face 26 is of a low-friction material, the vibration device 10 is held down and at the same time free to move over the exposed face 38, unlike a device that is gripped at one place. The vibration produced by the vibration motor 18 acts through the stirring elements 48 to produce a constant forward motion of the vibration device 10 over the exposed face 38. The vibration device 10 therefore advances from area to area of the covering element 36 without tension being applied to a flexible pulling element 46 and without being guided by hand, while the pressure differential is maintained throughout. The hold is not loosened to permit that motion: the air-extraction mechanism 20 continues to run and the pressure differential continues to press the bearing face 26 onto the exposed face 38 while the vibration device 10 advances, so the vibration coupling into the covering element 36 is not interrupted by the movement. The stirring elements 48 are shown schematically in FIG. 6.

In this embodiment the operator supplies neither the force that holds the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36 nor the force that moves it across the exposed face 38. The first is supplied by the pressure differential and the second by the vibration of the vibration device 10 acting through the stirring elements 48, so the vibration that is being delivered into the covering element 36 also carries the vibration device 10 over it.

Method of use

A method of bedding a covering element 36 into bonding material 40 using the vibration device 10 is carried out as follows. The method begins with placing the vibration device 10 on the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36, whereby the bearing face 26 of the perimeter member 24 is brought against the exposed face 38 so that the chamber 22 is bounded by the second side 16, the perimeter member 24 and the exposed face 38, with the clearance 34 remaining, along at least part of the perimeter member 24, between the bearing face 26 and the exposed face 38. It continues with operating the air-extraction mechanism 20 to withdraw air from the chamber 22 at a volumetric extraction rate sufficient to maintain the chamber 22 below atmospheric pressure while ambient air continues to enter the chamber 22 through the clearance 34, the resulting pressure differential holding the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36 without a downward force being required from the operator. It continues with operating the vibration motor 18 and transmitting vibration from the vibration motor 18 to the covering element 36 through the base 12 and the perimeter member 24 to the bearing face 26. It continues with translating the vibration device 10 across the exposed face 38, while the pressure differential is maintained, by sliding the bearing face 26 over the exposed face 38, so that vibration is delivered to successive areas of the covering element 36. The translating may be done by applying tension to the flexible pulling element 46, by guiding the vibration device 10 with the handle 44, or by the vibration acting through the stirring elements 48 to advance the vibration device 10 over the exposed face 38.

# FIG. 3 - Bottom plan view of the vibration device

**View:** Plan view looking straight up at the underside of the machine, nothing beneath the machine being drawn. Outline line work only; the only lettering drawn is the designation at each end of each section line, namely 2-2 at both ends of one and 4-4 at both ends of the other.

**Geometry to be drawn**

The sheet shows the underside of the machine as a rectangular ring in the manner of a picture frame. Two closed rectangular outlines appear in the view, one held within the other: the outer edge of the ring and the inner edge of the ring. The rectangular plan form is a depiction convention for this sheet only, both parts being shown schematically.

The perimeter member 24 is the ring surface. It runs continuously from the outer edge across to the inner edge, presenting one plain surface across its whole breadth, and it runs all the way round the four sides, carrying round each corner without interruption, so that it reads as one closed loop. It is broad along each of its four sides, broad enough for a point standing well inside it to be clear of both the outer edge and the inner edge; its breadth is schematic and no proportion is asserted.

The second side 16 is the face at which this view looks straight, and it appears as the area held within the inner edge of the ring. That area is one plain face, bounded on all four sides by the inner edge alone and running continuously from the inner edge on one side across to the inner edge on the opposite side. It is broad enough for a point standing well inside it to be clear of the inner edge all round.

Beyond the outer edge lies the surrounding background. The whole ring stands well inside the drawing area and is drawn large within it.

Two broken section lines are drawn across the view, each beginning and ending in the background just beyond the outer edge of the ring, each crossing the ring surface and the face within it, and each carrying an arrow at both ends showing the viewing direction and its designation at both ends. One runs horizontally with both arrows pointing toward the lower part of the sheet and is marked 2-2 at each end; it crosses the ring at two places where the perimeter member 24 bears on the covering element. The other runs vertically with both arrows pointing toward the left-hand part of the sheet and is marked 4-4 at each end; it crosses the ring at a place where the clearance is present. The section lines are drawing conventions only and assert no dimension or proportion.

- The perimeter member 24 is the ring surface lying between the outer edge and the inner edge. Identified well inside that surface along the left-hand side of the ring, clear of both edges.
- The second side 16 is the plain face held within the inner edge. Identified well inside that face, clear of the inner edge all round.

**Numerals appearing on this figure:** 16, 24

## Numerals shown on this figure

- 16
- 24
