input.summary: All three findings are fixed. Section designations now exist and match: the FIG. 3 brief draws two broken section lines, each beginning and ending in the background just beyond the outer edge of the ring, each crossing the ring surface and the face within it, each carrying an arrow at both ends and its designation at both ends; one runs horizontally with both arrows toward the lower part of the sheet, marked 2-2, crossing the ring where the perimeter member 24 bears on the covering element, and the other runs vertically with both arrows toward the left-hand part, marked 4-4, crossing where the clearance is present. Its View statement permits those designations as the only lettering. The same designations appear in the FIG. 2 and FIG. 4 brief View lines, in the Brief Description entries for FIG. 2 and FIG. 4, and in the detailed description. FIG. 1's numeral 10 is back on the outer boundary line, along the left-hand outer edge of the silhouette formed by the slab and the band together, clear of the front face and of the blocks, matching the convention used on FIG. 5 and FIG. 6, and the geometry sentence now describes that continuous outer boundary rather than an end face. Claim 15 now recites a second side opposite the first side and a perimeter member terminating, remote from the base, in the bearing face, matching claims 1 and 11 and the description. Compressions in FIG. 2 and FIG. 3 keep every brief at or below 2800 characters.
reasoning: The designation chain had to exist in three places at once, so I wrote it in all of them in one pass: the source-view brief draws and marks both lines, both resulting-view briefs name the line they are taken on, and the Brief Description and detailed description use the same phrase. A designation named in only one of those places is what left the earlier attempts unmatched.

The FIG. 3 lines are specified as drawing geometry rather than as bare labels: each has its start and end in the background beyond the ring, its alignment, the viewing direction of both arrows, and its designation repeated at both ends, and the brief states expressly that the lines are drawing conventions asserting no dimension or proportion. The View statement had to permit lettering again, limited to those designations, since a sheet cannot both print 2-2 and 4-4 and carry no lettering.

Placing 2-2 where the perimeter member bears on the covering element and 4-4 where the clearance is present matches what the text already says about the two planes, so the lines record a distinction the specification makes rather than introducing one.

On FIG. 1 I reverted my previous change. Moving numeral 10 inside the slab's left-hand end face cured a corner-vertex placement but created a worse problem, two numerals terminating inside surfaces of the same slab, so a reader could not tell which meant the assembly and which the base. The outer-boundary target is what FIG. 5 and FIG. 6 already use for numeral 10, and specifying that the slab and band present one continuous outer boundary on that side gives the leader a long edge to land on rather than a corner.

Claim 15 was the only independent claim missing the two relationships that claims 1 and 11 and the description use for the same parts. Adding opposite the first side and remote from the base removes the literal reading in which the sides are not opposed and the bearing face could be at either end, and it costs no scope that the description supports.

Both additions pushed briefs over the length limit, so I compressed wording that repeated what other sentences already carry, in FIG. 3 the four-sides restatements and in FIG. 2 three short phrases. Every body, contact, hatching assignment, section line and numeral endpoint survives, and all six briefs are at or below 2800 characters.

input.prior_art_strategy: Unchanged. Claim 1 rests on the rigid low-friction perimeter member at the perimeter of the second side, ending in a bearing face that leaves a clearance admitting ambient air continuously; an air-extraction mechanism whose volumetric rate holds the chamber below atmospheric against that ingress; an all-rigid transmission path with no elastomeric member, foam member or resilient mount interposed; and a bearing face slidable while the differential is maintained. Claim 15 now states the same base and perimeter-member relationships as claims 1 and 11, so the method claim cannot be read more loosely than the apparatus it performs. Claims 10 and 20 remain dependent and keep the recital that the device advances while the differential is maintained, distinguishing US-4934475-A, whose vibration reduces the suction-adhering hold to permit travel, and US-10001245-B2, which floats on a blower-fed air cushion to move. US-11247858-B2 remains lifting and cleaning equipment that delivers no vibration into a laid covering element.

# FIG. 3 - Bottom plan view of the vibration device

**View:** Plan view looking straight up at the underside of the machine, nothing beneath the machine being drawn. Outline line work only; the only lettering drawn is the numeral 2 at both ends of one section line and the numeral 4 at both ends of the other.

**Geometry to be drawn**

The sheet shows the underside of the machine as a rectangular ring in the manner of a picture frame. Two closed rectangular outlines appear in the view, one held within the other: the outer edge of the ring and the inner edge of the ring. The rectangular plan form is a depiction convention for this sheet only, both parts shown schematically.

The perimeter member 24 is the ring surface. It runs continuously from the outer edge across to the inner edge as one plain surface, and all the way round, carrying round each corner without interruption, so that it reads as one closed loop. It is broad along each side, broad enough for a point well inside it to be clear of both edges.

The second side 16 is the face at which this view looks straight, and it appears as the area held within the inner edge of the ring. That area is one plain face, bounded by the inner edge alone and continuous from that edge on one side across to the opposite side. It is broad enough for a point well inside it to be clear of the inner edge.

Beyond the outer edge lies background. The whole ring stands well inside the drawing area, drawn large within it.

Two broken section lines are drawn across the view. Each begins and ends in the background just beyond the outer edge of the ring and crosses the ring surface and the face within it.

The first line runs horizontally. It carries a short arrow at each of its two ends, both arrows pointing toward the lower part of the sheet, and the numeral 2 is drawn at each of its two ends, so that it reads as section line 2-2 and leads to the sectional view of FIG. 2. It crosses the ring where the perimeter member 24 bears on the covering element.

The other line runs vertically. It carries a short arrow at each of its two ends, both arrows pointing toward the left-hand part of the sheet, and the numeral 4 is drawn at each of its two ends, so that it reads as section line 4-4 and leads to the sectional view of FIG. 4. It crosses the ring where the clearance is present.

The section lines are drawing conventions only and assert no dimension or proportion.

- The perimeter member 24 is the ring surface lying between the outer edge and the inner edge. Identified well inside that surface along the left-hand side of the ring.
- The second side 16 is the plain face held within the inner edge. Identified well inside that face.

**Numerals appearing on this figure:** 16, 24

## Numerals shown on this figure

# FIG. 1 - Perspective view of the vibration device in use

**View:** Perspective view from above and to the front left. Outline line work only, with no lettering drawn.

**Geometry to be drawn**

The covering element 36 is one large plain tile in perspective filling the lower drawing area, the machine standing on its left-hand part with open tile to the right.

The machine is one plain rectangular slab, the base 12, standing on a band that runs round its underside. Three closed blocks stand side by side on the top face of the slab: the left-hand block is the vibration motor 18, the middle block is the handle 44, and the right-hand block is the air-extraction mechanism 20. Slab, band, blocks and tile are shown schematically, and the order and spacing of the three blocks is a placement convention for this sheet only, no particular handle form, size or mounting arrangement being asserted.

The slab is drawn thick, its front face turned toward the viewer as a large plain surface; its proportions are schematic. The view being taken from the front left, the left-hand end of the slab is also presented to the viewer, its outer edge standing upright from the band below to the top face above, so that the slab and the band together present one continuous outer boundary on that side.

Each block is drawn broad and tall, its front face turned toward the viewer.

The band meets the underside of the slab and follows the same rectangular run, its front surface facing the viewer as one unbroken strip across the whole width and drawn deep, a broad clear surface standing between the underside of the slab above and the tile below; its depth is schematic. It stands on the tile, its lower edge meeting the tile.

The whole of the drawing stands well inside the drawing area, the machine drawn large within it.

- The vibration device 10 is the whole machine, slab, blocks and band together. Identified on the outer boundary line of the machine along the left-hand outer edge of the silhouette formed by the slab and the band together, clear of the front face of the slab and clear of the blocks.
- The base 12 is the slab. Identified well inside its front face.
- The vibration motor 18 is the left-hand block. Identified well inside its front face.
- The air-extraction mechanism 20 is the right-hand block. Identified well inside its front face.
- The perimeter member 24 is the band beneath the slab. Identified well inside the front strip of the band, above the line along which the band meets the tile and below the line along which it meets the slab.
- The covering element 36 is the tile. Identified well inside the open tile to the right of the machine.
- The handle 44 is the middle block, standing between the other two. Identified well inside its front face.

input.summary: The request is the standing rebuild instruction, so the work this turn is the reported failure: numeral 24 landing in a rejected coordinate cluster on FIG. 1 and FIG. 6. Both sheets label the perimeter member on the band beneath the body, and FIG. 5 does the same successfully, so I fixed the two failing sheets by making the band a target the leader cannot miss and by clearing what crowds it. On both, the band's front strip is now specified as a broad clear surface whose upper and lower edges are well apart, and numeral 24 is identified well inside that strip between the line where the band meets the body and the line where it meets the tile, which is the two-boundary form FIG. 5 uses. On FIG. 6 the two stirring-element blocks are now drawn against the upper part of the front face, standing clear above the band, so nothing sits over the strip the leader must reach. Both briefs were trimmed to stay within the length limit, FIG. 1 at 2796 and FIG. 6 at 2757 characters. No claim, numeral definition, drawing description or disclosed embodiment changed, and no other figure brief was touched.
reasoning: The same numeral failed on the same part on two sheets while passing on FIG. 5, which shows the identical machine from the same viewpoint. That pointed at the depiction rather than the wording: where the band is drawn shallow, every candidate point falls close to one of its two edges, which is what a rejected cluster looks like.

So the repair went into the geometry first. The band's front strip is now required to be a broad clear surface with its upper and lower edges well apart along the whole width, which gives the endpoint an interior to land in instead of a sliver.

For the endpoint itself I adopted the two-boundary form that FIG. 5 uses and that passes there, naming the strip and the two lines that bound it. That is a broad interior region described by the part's own boundaries, not a coordinate or a fraction of the part.

FIG. 6 had a second cause that FIG. 1 does not: its two blocks were drawn against the front face of the body without any statement of where on that face, so they could be rendered low enough to sit over the band and crowd the target. They now stand against the upper part of the front face, clear above the band. That is a per-sheet depiction convention, and the brief still declares that no mounting face or position relative to the body or the perimeter member 24 is asserted, so the invention is untouched.

I did not move numeral 24 off either sheet. Dropping it would have satisfied the check while removing the label from the very part the claims turn on, and it would have forced the perimeter member out of both figure descriptions.

Both additions ran the briefs long, so I compressed wording that repeated what other sentences already carry, including the handle entry on FIG. 1 and the run description on both sheets. Every body, contact, convention disclaimer and numeral entry survives, and the numeral lists are unchanged.

The covering element 36 is one large plain tile seen in perspective, as in FIG. 1, filling the lower part of the drawing area. The machine stands on its left-hand part, with open tile to the right.

The machine and the tile are shown schematically, the machine as one plain rectangular body standing on a band that runs round its underside, the band alone touching the tile, these forms being a convention for this sheet only.

The band meets the underside of the body and follows the same rectangular run, its front surface facing the viewer as one unbroken strip across the whole width and drawn deep, a broad clear surface standing between the underside of the body above and the tile below, its upper and lower edges well apart; its depth is schematic. input.summary: The single finding is fixed with the suggested wording. The FIG. 6 paragraph on the stirring elements no longer instructs a position and then denies asserting one: it keeps the geometry, two small closed blocks each a stirring element 48 drawn carried by the machine against the upper part of the front face of the rectangular body, standing clear above the band, each broad enough for a point to stand well inside its front face, and now closes "They are shown schematically; their number, form and drawn position on this sheet are a depiction convention for this sheet only, no engagement with the covering element 36 being asserted." The renderer therefore has one consistent instruction, and the position is still labelled a convention rather than a disclosed relationship. Nothing else changed: the application text continues to say only that the vibration device 10 carries one or more stirring elements 48 and that they are shown schematically in FIG. 6, the sheet still carries numerals 10, 24, 36 and 48, and the brief is at 2691 characters.
reasoning: The contradiction came from my own repair two turns ago. I had moved the blocks to the upper part of the front face to stop them crowding numeral 24's target on the band, but left in place a disclaimer written for the earlier version that denied any position relative to the body or the perimeter member. Those two sentences cannot both be obeyed, and the renderer was being given a command and its negation together.

The right resolution is the one the finding sets out: keep the instruction, since the sheet must draw the blocks somewhere and that placement is what clears the band, and narrow the disclaimer to what it can honestly say, that the number, form and drawn position are a convention of this sheet.

I kept the clause about no engagement with the covering element 36, because that is a relationship the sources do not support and the drawing does not show, so denying it costs nothing and prevents the blocks being read as touching the work.

Dropping the disclaimer altogether was not an option: the inventor gave no appearance or location for the stirring elements, saying only that small stirring elements can be added and the vibrations cause a constant forward motion, so the drawn placement has to be marked as a depiction convention confined to the brief.

No text file needed touching. The detailed description still says only that the vibration device 10 carries one or more stirring elements 48 and that they are shown schematically in FIG. 6, and claims 10 and 20 remain location-neutral, so nothing in the application asserts where they sit.

I left the rest of the sheet alone, including the band geometry and the numeral 24 target repaired last turn, since neither was in question and re-editing them would risk the endpoint placement that repair was made to fix.
